claim: Zippia's creator economy statistics page — the source Goldman Sachs cites for its global creator population and its YouTube earnings-concentration figure — is an undated-methodology SEO listicle that reproduces figures originated by SignalFire, Linktree and NeoReach without attributing any of them.
stance_target: The evidentiary standing of the Goldman Sachs creator population model and every downstream citation of it
scope_conditions: Zippia page published 13 June 2023, last fact-checked 28 June 2023, bylined only 'Zippia Research'; no sample, no survey instrument, no primary data collection described anywhere on the page
quoted_support: There are an estimated 50 million people contributing to the creator economy, as of 2023. At least 46.7 million creators actually consider themselves amateurs.

claim: Zippia restates the YouTube concentration finding as '3% of YouTubers make 90% of the wealth', transforming a peer-reviewed measurement of view concentration into a claim about earnings that the underlying study never made.
stance_target: The claim that 3% of YouTube channels capture 90% of creator earnings
scope_conditions: YouTube; Zippia 2023 page; the peer-reviewed source (Bärtl, Convergence, 2018, DOI 10.1177/1354856517736979, 136 citations) reports that on average 85% of all views go to 3% of channels, a statement about attention, not revenue
quoted_support: 96.5% of YouTubers make less than $12,140 per year. YouTube is not an evenly split economy, as only 3% of YouTubes make 90% of the wealth.

claim: Zippia reports that roughly 2 million YouTube channels have more than 10,000 subscribers out of approximately 51 million channels as of 2022, implying only about 1.75% of channels reach that threshold.
stance_target: The claim that the overwhelming majority of channels never reach an audience scale compatible with monetization
scope_conditions: YouTube, 2022; Zippia aggregation with no stated primary source; channel counts include dormant and abandoned channels
quoted_support: Roughly 2 million YouTube channels have more than 10,000 subs. That equates to only 1.75% of the total channels on YouTube, meaning the average YouTuber only has a 1/57 chance of gaining more than 10,000 subs.

claim: Zippia's '$57,234 average annual US content creator salary' is a job-posting-derived wage estimate for employed content-creator roles, not a measure of independent creator earnings, yet it circulates alongside independent-creator statistics on the same page.
stance_target: The use of aggregator salary figures as evidence about what independent creators earn
scope_conditions: United States; Zippia salary-aggregator methodology built on employer job postings; incompatible with the same page's claim that most creators earn under a poverty-level income
quoted_support: In the U.S., the average content creator makes $57,234 per year. That would be the same as earning $27.52 per hour; however, the average could be considered skewed by the few at the top who make huge profits.

claim: Zippia's claim that creators earned an estimated $24.23 million in Patreon payouts in 2021 understates actual Patreon payouts by roughly two orders of magnitude, indicating a monthly-versus-annual unit error carried into a source Goldman Sachs relies on.
stance_target: The reliability of Zippia as a data source for creator earnings
scope_conditions: Patreon, 2021; Patreon publicly reported payouts on the order of $1bn per year by 2021, and Goldman's own 2025 exhibit shows monthly payouts in the tens of millions of dollars range
quoted_support: As of 2021, creators earned an estimated $24.23 million in Patreon payouts. That's more than a 26% increase from 2020, when payouts reached an estimated $19.19 million

claim: Zippia's Instagram follower distribution — claiming 24.3% of all Instagram accounts have more than 100,000 followers and only 9.1% have under 1,000 — is inconsistent with every measured account distribution and indicates a sample of influencer-tool-indexed accounts presented as the whole platform.
stance_target: The reliability of vendor follower-distribution statistics as population estimates
scope_conditions: Instagram; Zippia 2023 table; contrast with Linktree's estimate that only 2 million of 200 million creators globally have 1M+ followers
quoted_support: 24.3% of all Instagram accounts have more than 100,000 followers. That leaves 75.8% of accounts having less than 100,000.

claim: Zippia reports approximately 450,000 full-time creators as of 2020 while simultaneously reproducing Linktree's finding that only 12% of full-time creators earn over $50,000, implying roughly 54,000 people worldwide earned a US middle-class income from full-time content creation.
stance_target: The claim that the number of people making a genuine living from content creation is in the tens of thousands, not the millions
scope_conditions: 2020 creator count from an unstated source; the 12% figure originates in Linktree's 2021 survey of 9,576 users and is reused here without attribution; the arithmetic combination is this analysis's inference, not Zippia's
quoted_support: As of 2020, there are approximately 450,000 full-time creators. However, this doesn't mean that all of these full-time creators make a sizeable income. For example, only 12% of full-time creators make more than $50,000 per year.

claim: Zippia reports that only 31% of Patreon creators make more than $100 using the platform, a figure traceable to Patreon's own 2016 self-report and already obsolete by the time Zippia republished it in 2023.
stance_target: The currency of creator-earnings statistics recirculated by aggregators
scope_conditions: Patreon; the 31% figure derives from Patreon's 2016 disclosure of 7,960 creators over $100/month against ~25,000 creators, a ratio that collapsed as the platform grew past 79,000 creators by late 2017
quoted_support: Patreon is often sought out as an extra source of income. However, only 31% of creators make more than $100 using the platform.
numbers: 47.4% of Patreon members in video, podcasts, music, gaming
